name: The Ficus of the Plaza de la Encarnación
story: This tree is the last of eight, and it only got big because the city stopped cutting it. When the Plaza de la Encarnación was laid out around its old fountain, the design called for eight Indian laurel figs clipped into hard architectural shapes, a green wall of topiary around four cross-shaped beds. For reasons the city's own inventory admits it cannot explain, the clipping stopped. The crowns were allowed to run, and they ran: this one now carries a trunk 5.04 metres round, stands 27 metres tall and throws a crown 33 metres across, which is wider than the tree is high. Letting go had a cost. Unmanaged weight on roots that had nowhere good to go meant that storms took the others one at a time, snapping main limbs or tipping trees over root and all. Several of the ones that went over whole were dug up and given a second life in the Parque de Miraflores. Its size is misleading. It first appears in photographs of the plaza between 1948 and 1950, which makes it younger than plenty of people standing under it, and it now grows in the shadow of the Metropol Parasol, a structure most visitors come here to photograph instead.
transport: 8 min walk north from the Plaza Nueva tram stop (T1); buses on Calle Laraña
notes: Age, dimensions and planting window from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares de la Ciudad de Sevilla (2022), ficha 45, which states 72 years as of 2022 and first appearance in the plaza between 1948 and 1950. Coordinates are the catalogue's own WGS84 field and match Plaza de la Encarnación. City records physiological state Normal, phytosanitary state without anomalies, overall conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 8.

name: The Ficus of the Pila del Pato
story: A residents' association liked this tree enough to put it on their letterhead. The Indian laurel fig on the Plaza de San Leandro, known by the duck fountain it stands beside, was probably planted around 1945, going by photographs from the period. It survived the plaza's 1966 rebuild, when the bare earth square was paved over with cobbles and river stone, and the paving nearly finished it: the roots stopped getting air, branches died back from the tips, and the tree went into visible decline. The parks service drilled a ring of shafts around the root crown to let oxygen and nutrients back down, and it recovered fast. A bench built too close was later removed for the same reason. In 2019 the Asociación de Vecinos Casco Antiguo, working with the city, widened the planting pit and put new planting around it. The association took the tree as its logo, which is a fair summary of how the neighbourhood feels about it. It now measures 4.77 metres round with a crown 21 metres wide, and it has quietly reduced its own canopy over the years in response to the root damage, a tree editing itself down to what it can support.
transport: 12 min walk east from the Plaza Nueva tram stop (T1); buses on Calle Recaredo
notes: Planting date, 1966 paving, root drainage intervention, 2019 alcorque widening and the residents' association logo all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 20. The catalogue words the planting date as a probability from period photographs, so the age is given as a range. City records conservation Bueno, phytosanitary state without anomalies. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 11.

name: The Magnolia of the Cathedral

location.address: Avenida de la Constitución, beside Seville Cathedral, 41004 Sevilla

story: The best evidence for this tree's age is photographs it does not appear in. Shots taken from the Teatro Coliseo in 1931 and from the corner of the cathedral in 1934 show the spot empty, which puts the planting in the early 1940s and makes this magnolia a good deal younger than it looks standing against a Gothic wall begun in 1401. By the late 1960s it was well grown: it shows up in images from the years when the monument to the sculptor Juan Martínez Montañés stood here, between 1967 and 1985, before that statue moved to the Plaza del Salvador. Then the city nearly killed it by tidying up. The pedestrianisation of the Avenida de la Constitución in 2007 and the tram works that followed cut back its bed, compacted the ground and paved over the roots that were still doing the work. It declined so visibly that both the parks service and ordinary passers-by were alarmed. In June 2021 the city lifted the paving again, widened the pit and fed it. Seville's own inventory now rates it stressed but recovering, and the assessment is blunt about the cause: this was not weather or disease, it was the pavement.
transport: Archivo de Indias tram stop (T1) is 100 m away; Puerta de Jerez metro 5 min walk

best_time.label: May and June, when the cream flowers open the size of a spread hand

notes: Dating from absence in 1931 and 1934 photographs, the 1967-1985 Martinez Montanes monument period, the 2007 pedestrianisation damage and the June 2021 city intervention all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 24. The catalogue records physiological state Estresado (stressed) with overall conservation Bueno and notes the tree appears to be responding well to the 2021 works, so the decline is stated on the page rather than hidden. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 123396.

name: The Pecan of the Real Alcázar

location.address: Jardín del Marqués de la Vega Inclán, Real Alcázar de Sevilla, Patio de Banderas s/n, 41004 Sevilla

story: The tallest tree in the Alcázar gardens is a nut tree from the Mississippi valley, and almost nobody looks up at it. The pecan stands 37 metres in the Jardín del Marqués de la Vega Inclán, the garden José Gómez Millán laid out between 1913 and 1917 over what had been the Huerta del Retiro, the palace's working orchard. It was planted with the garden, alongside the other fruit trees Gómez Millán scattered through his design, so it is roughly as old as the layout around it. An older pecan grew near the Pabellón de Carlos V and was taken down when it became decrepit, which leaves this one carrying the species alone here. It is in unusually good order. Of the fifty-six individual trees in Seville's singular-tree inventory, this is one of a handful rated optimal on all three counts the city measures: physiological state, phytosanitary state and biomechanical structure. The inventory credits careful pruning over its whole life, and the fact that a planted border keeps visitors off the ground under its canopy. Its trunk is 2.8 metres round, its crown 24 metres across, and it fruits into autumn, though the nuts are not yours to gather.
access: Paid entry (Real Alcázar admission ticket required)
transport: 10 min walk from Puerta de Jerez tram stop (T1), inside the Real Alcázar grounds
notes: Garden dated 1913-1917 to Jose Gomez Millan, planting with the garden, the lost older specimen by the Pabellon de Carlos V, and the condition ratings all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 3. Age is given as a range because the catalogue dates the planting to the garden's construction window rather than to a year. City records physiological, phytosanitary and biomechanical state all Optimo, conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Real Alcazar de Sevilla. Height of 37 m is the tallest of the seven Alcazar trees in the catalogue; it is not the tallest tree in Seville, which the same catalogue records as El Gran Capitan at 55 m.

name: The Fig of the University Moat

location.address: Calle Palos de la Frontera, beside the University of Seville, 41004 Sevilla

story: A man in Seville asked the parks department in 1970 whether he could plant a tree to mark his son's birth. They said yes, brought a Moreton Bay fig to a bed on the Calle Palos de la Frontera, and let him throw the first spadefuls of earth in himself. That son turns fifty-six this year. So does the tree, and it has done rather better out of the arrangement: its trunk is now 6.12 metres round, thicker than any of the far older figs elsewhere in the city's inventory, and its crown spreads 28 metres, reaching out sideways over the dry moat of the old Royal Tobacco Factory, the eighteenth-century building that has housed the University of Seville since the 1950s. Moreton Bay figs grow like this. Native to the east coast of Australia, they drop aerial roots from their limbs, thicken fast in a warm climate and buttress out at the base until the trunk stops being a cylinder and becomes a set of fins. The city's inventory notes the odd habit of this one in particular, the way the canopy leans out over the ditch rather than filling out evenly. Fifty-six years is nothing for a tree. This one has not read the memo.
transport: 4 min walk from Puerta de Jerez metro and tram stop (T1); Prado de San Sebastián 8 min
notes: Planting year 1970, the circumstances of the planting, the dimensions and the observation about the crown leaning over the university moat all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 19. This is the most precisely dated tree of the eight because the catalogue records the year and the reason. City records physiological state Optimo, phytosanitary state without anomalies, conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 55.

name: The Lagunaria of the Espacio Lope de Vega

location.address: Antiguos jardines de San Telmo (La Madrina), beside the Teatro Lope de Vega, Avenida María Luisa, 41013 Sevilla

story: Spanish calls this tree the pica-pica, the itching tree, and the name is a warning rather than a joke. Its seed capsules are packed with fine hairs that lodge in skin and sting for hours, which is why you should admire the pods and leave them alone. Everything else about it is generous. It came from Norfolk Island in the Pacific, it holds its grey-green leaves all year, and at the turn from spring into summer it hangs itself with pale pink bells, solitary in the leaf axils, over a period of weeks. This one is a survivor of the gardens the Duke and Duchess of Montpensier laid out at the Palacio de San Telmo after they took the palace in 1849, when they turned its grounds into one of the great private gardens of nineteenth-century Spain. Most of that garden was later carved up: a large part became the Parque de María Luisa when the Infanta gave it to the city in 1893, and the fragment this tree stands in, known as La Madrina, now sits beside the Teatro Lope de Vega. Seville's inventory lists it among the older trees in the city. It is 22 metres tall, with a trunk 2.75 metres round that branches from the base.
transport: 5 min walk from Prado de San Sebastián tram and metro interchange, beside the Teatro Lope de Vega

best_time.label: May into June, when the pale pink bells open across the whole crown

notes: Montpensier-era origin, flowering period, the irritant seed hairs and the dimensions from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 40. The age is the widest range of the eight because the catalogue dates it only to the Montpensier plantings, which ran from 1849 into the 1890s; it is deliberately not stated more precisely. The catalogue's phrase is that it figures among the oldest trees in Seville, which is reported here as the city's assessment rather than asserted as a record, since the Ombu of La Cartuja on this same page is estimated at 500 years. City records physiological state Optimo, conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla.

name: The Ficus of the Altozano
story: Triana's landmark tree began as a pot plant. The city kept large containerised specimens for dressing streets and squares during civic celebrations, and in 1972, when the monument to the bullfighter Juan Belmonte was inaugurated on the Plaza del Altozano, one of those container plants was put into the ground and left there. It is a rubber fig, and specifically the variety that was fashionable as a houseplant in the same decade, the kind that sat in a corner of a thousand Spanish living rooms. Seville's run of mild winters let this one keep going outdoors. Fifty-four years on it has a trunk 5.86 metres round and a crown 31 metres across, which covers both halves of the square at once: the approach to the Puente de Isabel II, successor to the old bridge of boats, and the mouth of the Calle Betis running downriver. The city's inventory is candid that the tree is not especially old and says its value here is symbolic. It has paid for that status. Every year the Velá de Triana sets its stalls up around the trunk, and in some years cooks put stoves underneath, badly enough to burn the bark.
transport: 10 min walk from Plaza Nueva tram stop (T1) across the Puente de Isabel II; buses to Plaza del Altozano
notes: Planting year 1972 tied to the inauguration of the Juan Belmonte monument, the origin as a municipal container plant, the Ficus elastica var. decora identification, the Vela de Triana stall damage and the dimensions all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 18. The catalogue itself notes the tree is not especially old and rests its case on symbolic value and size, which the story states rather than dresses up. City records physiological state Normal, phytosanitary state without anomalies, conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 8 in the Triana lot.

name: The Pineapple Guava of the Plaza de Santa Cruz
story: Children in this square have known for a century that the green fruit on it tastes of pineapple. The pineapple guava normally stops at a shrub of four or five metres. This one reached six, and it did so because it has been left alone since about 1921, when the architect Juan Talavera laid out the Plaza de Santa Cruz on ground cleared by the demolition of a church and planted the garden that still frames it. At the centre he set the Cruz de la Cerrajería, a wrought-iron cross forged in 1692 by Sebastián Conde, a blacksmith from Almonte, which had already been moved twice, from the corner of Calles Sierpes and Rioja to the Museo de Bellas Artes and finally here. The guava went in with the rest of the planting and has outlasted most of it. Its flowers are the show nobody expects from a fruit bush: white petals curled back around a crown of red stamens tipped with bright yellow pollen, held on the branch for weeks. The fruit needs a second tree's pollen to set, comes in a little larger than a medlar, and is what the neighbourhood remembers it for.
transport: 6 min walk east from Seville Cathedral, through the Santa Cruz quarter; Archivo de Indias tram stop (T1) 8 min

best_time.label: October into November, when the fruit ripens and drops

notes: The 1921 laying out of the square by Juan Talavera with this feijoa included in the planting, the 1692 cross by Sebastian Conde and its earlier locations, the flower description and the pineapple taste of the fruit all from the Ayuntamiento de Sevilla's Inventario de Arboles Singulares (2022), ficha 52. The catalogue uses the older name Feijoa sellowiana; Acca sellowiana is the currently accepted name and is used here for species-page grouping. Smallest of the eight at 6 m and 78 cm girth, catalogued for rarity and age rather than size: the catalogue notes the species is usually a 4 to 5 m shrub. City records physiological, phytosanitary and biomechanical state all Optimo, conservation Bueno. Titularidad: Ayuntamiento de Sevilla, Arbomap id 4.
